name: Soft 3D
basis: 3D render style: shapes puffed and lit softly (how)

lumenary.blurb: A toy-like render: every shape swells like soft vinyl, is lit from above, throws a small shadow on its neighbour and carries a sheen, in the pale colours of a studio set.

facts.bestOn: Simple scenes with a few large shapes

why: Soft 3D illustration makes everything look like an inflatable toy: no hard corners, pale colour, light that seems to come from a studio softbox. The trick is that shape is shown by shading alone. Here each area of the picture is treated as its own cushion, puffed up from its outline, lit from above and given a sheen.
how: Simplify the picture into a few flat shapes.
Give each shape height: zero at its outline, rising inward to a level top.
Work out which way the surface faces at every pixel from the slope of that height.
Light it softly from above, so the shaded side stays light.
Add a tight highlight and a broad one, darken the seams and drop small shadows.
history: The shading comes from early computer graphics: Bui Tuong Phong described his highlight model in 1975 and Jim Blinn simplified it in 1977. The look is recent. Vinyl designer toys appeared in Hong Kong and Japan in the late 1990s, and around 2020 free 3D software put soft, rounded, pastel renders within reach of illustrators, who used them across apps, advertising and editorial work.
terms: A direction pointing straight out of a surface.
The bright spot where a shiny surface mirrors the light.
The darkening of creases and corners where less light reaches.
paragraphs: The picture is first simplified into a handful of flat shapes: smoothing that keeps edges, a small palette found by k-means, and a majority filter that rounds the shapes off. Height is then invented for each shape. A map that is 0 on every outline and 1 elsewhere is blurred twice, so the zeros spread inward as a slope, and the result is raised to the power 2.2. Each shape ends up with the cross-section of a cushion: low at the seam, level in the middle. The inflation slider sets the blur radius, that is, how far in from the seam the swelling reaches.

The slopes of that height map give a surface normal at every pixel, and the normal is lit. Diffuse light is wrapped, so the side turned away from the lamp is dim, not black, as on a soft translucent toy. The sheen is the Blinn-Phong highlight computed twice, once tight and once broad. Seams are darkened, each shape drops a small shadow on its neighbour on the side away from the light, and a rim of cool light is added where the surface turns away from the viewer. The colour underneath is four parts flat paint to one part smoothed picture, so faces keep a little of their gradient.

equations.note: Height: B² is two box blurs of the given radius; r runs from 4 to 11 pixels with the inflation slider.
Wrapped diffuse light from the normal n, built from the slopes of h, and the light direction l.

equations.tex: s=g\,\big(0.85\,(\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf h)^{46}+0.12\,(\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf h)^{7}\big),\qquad \mathbf h=\frac{\mathbf l+\mathbf v}{\lvert\mathbf l+\mathbf v\rvert}
equations.note: Sheen: a tight and a broad highlight around the half vector h; v points at the viewer, g is the sheen slider.

presets.text: Full inflation and sheen give a balloon animal.
Fewer, simpler shapes read best at small sizes.
No pastel and light from the right is closer to glazed clay.
